diagram.title: Python synchronous vs asynchronous Playwright APIs — step by step

steps.label: 10.1 Storytelling: One receptionist vs overlapping requests
steps.narration: A synchronous receptionist finishes handling one request before proceeding with the next operation.

steps.label: 10.2 Python synchronous API
steps.narration: Each synchronous API call waits until that operation completes before returning control to your surrounding Python code.

steps.label: 10.5 Method-by-method comparison
steps.narration: Notice that not every method in an asynchronous API needs await. Constructing a locator is synchronous because it creates a query description, not an immediate browser action.

steps.label: 10.6 Concurrent execution with separate pages
steps.narration: Suppose an AI research workflow needs to inspect three approved web pages.

steps.label: Sequential vs concurrent browser tasks
steps.narration: Idealized timings with independent pages and no resource contention. Asynchronous code does not guarantee faster execution under every workload.

steps.label: 10.8 When should you use sync or async Python?
steps.narration: Python's recommended pytest integration also supports asynchronous fixture workflows through the appropriate async plugin.

sections.title: Headed vs headless execution
sections.body:
## 11.1 Storytelling

Headed mode is like watching a driver operate a car.

Headless mode is like receiving instructions and results from an automated driver without watching the physical driving interface.

Both execute browser operations. The main distinction is whether the browser presents its ordinary graphical window.

**Headed**

Visible browser window. Helpful for debugging.

**Headless**

Without an ordinary browser window. Common in CI/CD.

## 11.2 Python

```python
browser = p.chromium.launch(
    headless=False,
    slow_mo=500
)
```

## 11.3 TypeScript

```typescript
const browser = await chromium.launch({

    headless: false,

    slowMo: 500
});
```

The slow-motion option delays Playwright operations for observation.

It is a debugging aid, not a synchronization strategy.

## 11.4 Comparison

| Feature | Headed | Headless |
|--------|--------|--------|
| Browser GUI | Visible | No ordinary browser window |
| Debugging interactions | Convenient | Use traces/screenshots/logs |
| CI/CD | Requires display support as applicable | Common default |
| Screenshots | Supported | Supported |
| Browser JavaScript | Executes | Executes |
| Performance | Workload-dependent | Workload-dependent |

A headless browser still loads pages, executes JavaScript, performs rendering and communicates over the network.

It is not equivalent to Python `requests` or Node.js `fetch`, which do not provide an entire browser environment.

Your first complete browser automation script
Automation script vs automated test
sections.body:
These two terms are related but not identical.

Consider this script:

```python
page.goto("https://example.com")

print(page.title())
```

It automates a browser operation, but it does not verify a business expectation.

Now add:

```python
expect(page).to_have_title("Example Domain")
```

This makes the operation capable of reporting a verification failure.

A formal automated test usually also runs within a test runner that provides test discovery, reporting, fixtures, lifecycle management and optional parallelism.

## 14.1 First Python automated test with pytest

Create `tests/test_first.py`:

```python
from playwright.sync_api import Page, expect

def test_example_domain(page: Page):

    page.goto("https://example.com")

    expect(page).to_have_title(
        "Example Domain"
    )

    expect(

        page.get_by_role(
            "heading",
            name="Example Domain"
        )

    ).to_be_visible()
```

Run:

```bash
pytest
```

Run in headed mode:

```bash
pytest --headed
```

Run a particular file:

```bash
pytest tests/test_first.py -v
```

Run on Firefox:

```bash
pytest --browser firefox
```

## 14.2 First TypeScript automated test

Create `tests/first.spec.ts`:

```typescript
import {
    test,
    expect
} from "@playwright/test";

test("Verify Example Domain", async ({ page }) => {

    await page.goto("https://example.com");

    await expect(page)
        .toHaveTitle("Example Domain");

    await expect(

        page.getByRole(
            "heading",
            { name: "Example Domain" }
        )

    ).toBeVisible();
});
```

Run:

```bash
npx playwright test
```

Run in headed mode:

```bash
npx playwright test --headed
```

Run a particular test file:

```bash
npx playwright test tests/first.spec.ts
```

Open the interactive test UI:

```bash
npx playwright test --ui
```

## 14.3 Where does the page come from?

You may have noticed that the test never explicitly launches the browser.

Python:

```python
def test_example_domain(page):
```

TypeScript:

```typescript
test("Example", async ({ page }) => {
```

The `page` is a fixture provided by the testing infrastructure.

Both standard integrations provide isolated page fixtures, with browser contexts separating test environments. 

This is dependency injection, which we learned during the TypeScript OOP module.
